extractions.source_title: Bacterial Black Spot (BBS) of Mango in Florida

disease_name.evidence: Bacterial black spot (BBS), also known as bacterial canker, is caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Bacterial black spot is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae (Gagnevin and Pruvost 2001, Ah-You et al. 2009).

type_of_disease.evidence: Bacterial black spot is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae

affected_parts.evidence: The causal agent of BBS (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae) infects stems, leaves, and fruit tissue through natural openings and wounds

summary.value: Leaf lesions appear as raised black angular spots with greasy margins following leaf venation, often surrounded by a chlorotic (yellow) halo. Fruit lesions begin as small irregular water-soaked specks or star-shaped lesions around lenticels that blacken, develop raised greasy margins, coalesce, and crack.
summary.evidence: Leaf lesions appear as raised black angular spots, frequently developing greasy margins following leaf venation, and often surrounded by a chlorotic (yellow) halo. Symptoms on fruits begin as small irregular water-soaked specks around lenticels or as small star-shaped lesions. As the disease progresses, these lesions blacken, develop greasy margins that become raised and coalesce, and then develop cracks.

diagnostic_features.value: BBS lesions are angular and raised (not round and sunken), confined to the peel and upper pulp, darker, with raised margins that crack and ooze sap when coalescing. A tear-stain infection pattern may also occur.
diagnostic_features.evidence: BBS lesions are generally confined to the peel and upper pulp, are darker and more angular, and have raised margins. Additionally, when BBS lesions coalesce, they form cracks from which sap oozes out. Note that these necrotic spots are angular and raised, not round and depressed into the pulp like anthracnose lesions.

look_alikes.evidence: BBS symptoms may be confused with those caused by the common anthracnose fungus, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, a pathogen that is widespread and ubiquitous in Florida mango groves.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Infection of mango trees with the fungus Botryosphaeria rhodina

affected_parts.evidence: young twigs start withering at the base, extending outwards until the leaves become affected. As the veins turn brown, leaves curl upwards and eventually fall off the tree. It invades the vascular system of mango trees through wounds in the trunk and branches.

summary.value: Bark darkens and discolors in early stages; twigs wither and leaves curl upward then fall off; gum secretion appears on twigs and branches in later stages.
summary.evidence: During the first stage of the disease, the barks become discolored and turn darker. In the following stages, young twigs start withering at the base, extending outwards until the leaves become affected. As the veins turn brown, leaves curl upwards and eventually fall off the tree. In the final stages of dieback, twigs and branches secrete gum.

diagnostic_features.value: Gum secretion from twigs and branches is a key later-stage sign; initially small gum droplets appear, progressing to coverage of entire branches or trunk; bark and branches may die and crack in severe cases.
diagnostic_features.evidence: In the final stages of dieback, twigs and branches secrete gum. Initially, small gum droplets become visible, but as the disease progresses the entire branch or trunk may be covered. In severe cases, the tree bark or whole branches die and crack.

disease_name.evidence: Common Name Mango anthracnose, mango blossom blight

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Scientific Name Glomerella cingulata (it also has the name of Colletotrichum gloeosporioides ). Glomerella is the sexual stage of the fungus, and Colletotrichum the asexual stage.

type_of_disease.evidence: so fungi that produce dark spots are often given this name

affected_parts.evidence: It causes a blight of flowers and young shoots, leaf spots, and fruit rots.

summary.value: Spots start small, black, and irregular on leaves, expanding into large dead areas that dry and fall out. On mature fruit, infections form dark brown to black spots with orange-pink spore masses as the fruit ripens.
summary.evidence: At first, the spots are small, black and irregular, often expanding to form large dead areas that dry and fall out. On mature fruits, the fungus remains as pinpoint infections until the fruit ripens; then the infections form dark brown to black spots with orange-pink spore masses

diagnostic_features.value: Glomerella spots on leaves are usually larger than Stigmina spots. On fruit, orange-pink spore masses develop in the centres of dark brown to black spots.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Spots of Glomerella are usually larger on the leaves, whereas those of Stigmina are about 6 mm diameter, surrounded by a wide light greenish zone

look_alikes.evidence: it is not always easy to distinguish between diseases caused by Glomerella and Stigmina . Spots of Glomerella are usually larger on the leaves, whereas those of Stigmina are about 6 mm diameter, surrounded by a wide light greenish zone (Photos 3-5)

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: the causal agent of the mango dieback disease in the UAE is L. theobromae

type_of_disease.evidence: different fungi associated with it ... Fungal pathogens, such as Neofusicoccum ribis, Botryosphaeria dothidea ... L. theobromae is a soil-borne wound pathogen

affected_parts.evidence: The pathogen was observed to attack different parts of the mango trees. First, we noticed the disease symptoms in all plant tissues, including leaves, twigs, and apical tips ... discolouration of vascular regions of the stems and branches ... resulting in the eventual death of the whole tree

summary.value: Leaves roll upward and turn brown with a scorch-like appearance, then drop; twigs die back from tips inward toward vascular tissues. In advanced stages, branches dry out sequentially, vascular tissues brown, and the whole tree is defoliated and dies.
summary.evidence: leaves, their margins roll upwards turning them a brownish colour. Later, a scorch-like appearance developed, followed by the dropping of the infected leaves. Moreover, twigs died from the tips back inwards (toward the vascular tissues), giving a scorched appearance to the branches ... branches dry out one after another in a sequence resulting in the eventual death of the whole tree

diagnostic_features.value: Twig tip dieback advancing inward with browning of vascular tissues visible on cross-section, combined with leaf margin rolling, browning, and scorch-like defoliation; symptoms progress sequentially branch by branch.
diagnostic_features.evidence: twigs died from the tips back inwards (toward the vascular tissues) ... We observed browning in the vascular tissues when longitudinal cross-sections were made in diseased mango twigs ... twig tip dieback that advances into the old wood with branches that dry and die, and leaves scorch and fall

extractions.source_title: Sooty moulds (051) - Lucid Apps (Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds)

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: A number of sooty mould fungi have been identified in Pacific island countries; e.g., those from Solomon Islands - mostly from living leaves - are as follows: Aithaloderma citri (grapefruit); Capnodium citri (citrus); Capnodium mangiferum (mango);

type_of_disease.evidence: There are many fungal species, mostly saprophytes (i.e., non-pathogens) that form sooty mould deposits on trees and shrubs

affected_parts.evidence: large amounts of honeydew, and dense growths of sooty mould fungi over leaves and stems (Photos 1-4)

summary.value: Sooty moulds appear as dark, superficial fungal deposits on leaves and stems. They grow on honeydew secreted by sap-sucking insects and do not penetrate plant tissue.
summary.evidence: The fungi that cause sooty moulds grow on the sugary substances that are produced by insects... The leaf is still green beneath the superficial mould.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark sooty deposits on the upper surface of leaves and stems; the leaf remains green beneath the superficial mould layer; presence of sap-sucking insects (aphids, soft scale, leafhoppers, planthoppers, psyllids, whiteflies) is typically associated.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The leaf is still green beneath the superficial mould. ... Often, their presence is a sign that sap-sucking insects are present... The fungi that cause sooty moulds grow on the sugary substances that are produced by insects - mostly, aphids, soft scale (not armoured scale), leafhoppers, planthoppers, psyllids and whiteflies
